rewritten_text:
I don’t rush straight at him and risk making a clumsy job of it. No, I start well off to one side and work my way toward him slowly, so he never suspects I mean to strike. Then, all at once, he is flat on his back, with no idea in the world how he got there. That was how I tackled brother Dowley. I began speaking in a lazy, comfortable way, as though I merely wanted to fill the time. The oldest man alive could not have guessed, from where I started, where I intended to end up:

‘Boys, there are plenty of curious things about laws and customs and everyday habits, once you examine them. The same goes for the way people’s opinions change and human affairs move forward. Written laws disappear; unwritten laws last forever. Consider the unwritten law of wages: it says they must rise, little by little, century after century. Here is how it works. We know what people earn now in different places, so we work out an average and call that today’s wage. We know what wages were a hundred years ago, and two hundred years ago. That is as far back as our information goes, but it is enough to show us the rule of their growth: how much they rise, and how quickly. So, even without records, we can make a fairly close estimate of wages three, four, and five hundred years ago. So far, so good. But do we stop there? No. We turn away from the past and apply the same rule to the future. My friends, name any future date you please, for hundreds and hundreds of years ahead, and I can tell you what people will earn.’

‘What is that you say, my good man?’

‘Yes. Seven hundred years from now, wages here in your district will be six times their present level. Farm workers will be paid three cents a day, and skilled workers six.’

‘I wish I could die now and be alive then!’ interrupted Smug the wheelwright, his eyes shining with greed.

‘And that is not all. They will get their meals as well—such meals as they are; nobody will grow fat on them. Two hundred and fifty years after that—listen carefully—a skilled worker’s daily wage will be twenty cents! Remember, this follows a law; I am not guessing.’

Everyone gasped in amazed wonder. Dickon the mason raised his eyes and hands, and murmured:

‘Is that all? That is hardly much! Plenty of people have offended the Republic and must look through the little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he?’

‘I am. I must be, since I am the last.’

Jarvis Lorry has answered every previous question. Jarvis Lorry has stepped down and stands with one hand on the carriage door, answering a group of officials. They stroll around the carriage, then climb unhurriedly onto the driver’s seat to inspect the small amount of baggage on the roof. The country people gathered nearby crowd closer to the doors and stare hungrily inside. A mother holds out the short arm of the child she carries, so that it can touch the wife of an aristocrat who has gone to the Guillotine.

‘Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, countersigned.’

‘May we leave, citizen?’

‘You may leave. Forward, riders! Have a good journey!’

‘My respects, citizens.—And we have passed the first danger!’

Again it is Jarvis Lorry speaking, clasping his hands and looking upward. Inside the carriage there is terror, there are tears, there is the heavy breathing of the unconscious traveler.

‘Aren’t we moving too slowly? Can’t they be persuaded to go faster?’ Lucie asks, clinging to the old man.

‘It would look as though we were escaping, my darling. I must not press them too hard; that would arouse suspicion.’

‘Look behind us, look behind us, and see whether anyone is following!’

‘The road is empty, my dearest. So far, no one is following.’

Houses pass in groups of two and three, isolated farms, ruined buildings, dye works, tanneries and similar places, open fields, avenues of bare trees. Beneath us is the hard, uneven paving; on either side, deep, soft mud. Sometimes we turn into that bordering mud to escape the stones that rattle and jolt us; sometimes we become trapped there in ruts and boggy patches. Then the torment of our impatience becomes so fierce that, frantic with fear and haste, we want to jump out and run, hide, do anything at all except remain still.

We leave the open fields and enter another stretch of ruined buildings, isolated farms, dye works and tanneries, cottages in twos and threes, avenues of bare trees. Have these men tricked us, returning by a different road? Are we passing the same place again? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look behind us, look behind us—are we being followed? Quiet! The horse-changing station.

Unhurriedly, they unharness our four horses. Unhurriedly, the carriage waits in the little street, without horses and seemingly without any prospect of ever moving again. Unhurriedly, fresh horses appear, one at a time. Unhurriedly, the new riders follow, sucking and braiding their whip lashes. Unhurriedly, the old riders count their money, add it up incorrectly, and reach totals that leave them dissatisfied.

Elizabeth was sad and dispirited. Her usual activities no longer gave her pleasure; any enjoyment seemed a desecration of the dead. At that time she believed endless grief and tears were the proper tribute to innocence so cruelly ruined. She was no longer the happy girl who had walked beside the lake with me when we were younger, speaking ecstatically about our future. The first of those sorrows that loosen our attachment to the world had reached her, and its shadow had extinguished her sweetest smiles.

‘When I think, my dear cousin,’ she said, ‘of Justine Moritz’s miserable death, the world and everything in it look different to me. Before, the accounts of wickedness and injustice I read or heard seemed like stories from ancient times, or evils someone had invented. At least they were distant: my mind understood them, but my imagination could scarcely grasp them. Now suffering has reached our own home, and people seem like monsters thirsting for one another’s blood. Yet surely I am being unfair. Everyone believed that poor girl guilty; and if she had committed the crime she died for, she would indeed have been among the most corrupt human beings. To murder the son of her benefactor and friend for a few jewels—a child she had cared for since birth, and seemed to love as her own! I could never agree to anyone’s execution, but I would certainly have considered such a person unfit to live among others. Yet she was innocent. I know it, I feel it; and you believe it too, which strengthens my conviction. Oh, Victor, when a lie can look so much like truth, how can anyone feel sure of happiness? I feel as though I am walking along a cliff’s edge, with thousands pressing toward me, trying to push me into the depths. William and Justine have been murdered, and their murderer escapes. He moves freely through the world, perhaps even enjoying people’s respect. But even if I were sentenced to die on the scaffold for those same crimes, I would never exchange places with that wretched man.’

I listened in unbearable anguish. Though I had not performed the acts, I was in effect the real murderer. Elizabeth saw the agony in my face and gently took my hand. ‘My dearest friend,’ she said, ‘you must try to calm yourself. God knows how deeply these events have hurt me, but I am not as miserable as you are.’
